title: useEffect and Component Lifecycle
description: Master useEffect by understanding component mount/unmount, cleanup functions, and dependency arrays with non-primitive values. Learn when effects run, how to prevent infinite loops, and best practices for managing side effects in React components.

steps.title: Import useEffect and Add Mount Effect
steps.explanation:
useEffect is React's hook for handling side effects - code that needs to interact with the outside world (APIs, timers, DOM, subscriptions). Unlike render logic which must be pure, effects let you synchronize your component with external systems.

Effects run AFTER React finishes rendering and updating the DOM. This timing is crucial: your component renders first, the DOM updates, then your effect runs. This ensures you're working with the latest DOM state.

The basic pattern is simple: call useEffect and pass a function. This function runs after every render by default. Think of it as saying "after you finish rendering, do this side effect."
steps.task:
1. Import useEffect from 'react' (add it to your existing import)
2. Inside your component, call useEffect with a function that logs 'Component mounted' to the console
3. This effect will run after every render - we'll optimize this in the next step
hints: Add useEffect to the import: import { useState, useEffect } from 'react'
Call useEffect inside your component, before the return statement
Pass a function to useEffect: useEffect(() => { console.log('Component mounted') })

steps.title: Control When Effect Runs with Dependency Array
steps.explanation:
By default, effects run after EVERY render. This is rarely what you want. The dependency array lets you control when your effect runs by specifying which values it depends on.

An empty dependency array [] means "run this effect only once, after the initial mount." This is perfect for setup code that should happen once when the component appears (like fetching initial data or setting up subscriptions).

Think of the dependency array as answering: "What values does this effect care about?" If the answer is "nothing, just run it once," use []. If it depends on props or state, list them in the array.
steps.task:
Add an empty dependency array [] as the second argument to your useEffect call.

This tells React: "Only run this effect once after the component first mounts, then never again."
hints: useEffect takes two arguments: a function and an array
The empty array goes after the function: useEffect(() => { ... }, [])
The [] means this effect has no dependencies, so it runs only once

steps.title: Add Cleanup Function for Unmount
steps.explanation:
Effects can return a cleanup function. This function runs when the component unmounts OR before the effect runs again. Cleanup is essential for preventing memory leaks and bugs.

Common use cases for cleanup: clearing timers, canceling network requests, unsubscribing from events, removing event listeners. Without cleanup, these keep running even after your component is gone.

The cleanup timing is precise: React calls your cleanup BEFORE running the effect again, and when the component unmounts. This ensures you clean up the old effect before starting the new one.
hints: Your effect function should return another function
The returned function is the cleanup - it runs when the component unmounts

steps.title: Add State and Track Changes with Dependencies
steps.explanation:
When your effect needs to respond to changing values (props or state), list them in the dependency array. React compares the current values to the previous render's values. If any changed, the effect runs again.

This is how you create effects that "react" to changes. The effect re-runs whenever its dependencies change, keeping your side effects in sync with your component's data.

Critical rule: if you use a value inside your effect, it MUST be in the dependency array. Otherwise you'll have stale values and bugs. Modern tooling (ESLint with react-hooks plugin) will warn you about missing dependencies.
steps.task:
1. Add a new state variable called 'count' initialized to 0 (use useState)
2. Add a button that increments count when clicked
3. Create a NEW useEffect (in addition to your mount/unmount one) that:
   - Logs 'Count changed to: ' followed by the count value
   - Has [count] as its dependency array (runs whenever count changes)
4. Display the count in your JSX
hints: You'll have TWO useEffect calls now - one with [] and one with [count]
In the button's onClick, call setCount with count + 1
The second effect should log the count and have [count] in its dependency array

steps.title: Handle Object Dependencies Correctly
steps.explanation:
Here's a critical pitfall: React compares dependencies using Object.is(), which means objects and arrays are compared by REFERENCE, not by value. Even if an object's contents are identical, if it's a new object instance, React sees it as changed.

This causes infinite loops! If you create a new object/array in your component body and put it in dependencies, it's recreated every render. Effect runs, component re-renders, new object created, effect runs again - infinite loop.

Solutions: (1) Move objects outside component if they don't depend on props/state, (2) Use individual primitive values instead of objects, (3) Use useCallback/useMemo to stabilize references, (4) Sometimes you need to compare object properties individually.
steps.task:
1. Create a new state variable 'user' that holds an object: { name: 'Alice', age: 25 }
2. Add a button that updates the user's age (create a new object with ...user, age: user.age + 1)
3. Create a useEffect that logs the user's name
4. Put user.name (NOT user) in the dependency array - this way it only runs when the name actually changes, not when any part of the object changes
5. Display the user's name and age in your JSX
hints: useState({ name: 'Alice', age: 25 }) creates the user object state
This way the effect only runs when the name changes, not the age
